taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native range Texas to Mexico. Older literature may list it as Commelina anomala, Commelinantia anomala, or Tradescantia anomala.
look_here_first: Look below the whole flower cluster: Tinantia anomala has an exposed, one-sided cyme above an open, mostly flat leaflike bract. The green sepals around individual buds are not a fused spathe pocket. Then check Joey's macro for purple-and-yellow filament beards: six fertile stamens, five filaments bearded. Commelina erecta instead has a folded spathe pocket and smooth filaments.

project_inclusion.range_basis: BONAP/NAPA provides a county map for Tinantia anomala and Kew/POWO accepts Texas in the native range. Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Commelinaceae herbarium index includes Tinantia anomala. Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed county treatment for Tinantia anomala. Val Verde County — the Amistad National Recreation Area vascular flora documents Tinantia anomala on rocky slopes, flats, ledges, and intermittent drainages.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Tinantia anomala is an annual and may colonize garden settings. County proof uses herbarium/floristic evidence, not horticultural occurrences.

best_field_traits: annual, tufted to several-stemmed herb, commonly up to about 60–80 cm
stems cylindrical rather than strongly flattened, often pinkish-purple near exposed nodes
basal/lower leaves narrower and often petiolate; upper cauline leaves broader and sessile
upper leaf bases often rounded to cordate-clasping around the stem
terminal one-sided cyme with several flowers
large subtending bract is leaflike and mostly flat/open rather than forming a closed fused spathe pocket
flowers about 2–2.7 cm across with two broad blue-to-lavender petals and a much smaller white lower petal
six stamens are fertile and heteromorphic; several filaments have conspicuous violet/yellow-tipped beadlike hairs
persistent boat-shaped sepals conceal the developing capsule
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Commelina erecta: Commelina erecta has the unmistakable folded/fused green spathe pocket enclosing buds and fruit. Tinantia instead has an open leaflike bract subtending an exposed terminal cyme; its upper leaves also more strongly clasp the stem. Tradescantia spp.: Tradescantia spiderworts usually have three comparably showy petals. Tinantia has two large blue/lavender petals plus one much smaller white petal, and its one-sided cyme/bract architecture differs. Commelina benghalensis: Tropical spiderwort/dayflower is an invasive Commelina with a true spathe and often reddish hairs on leaf sheaths. Tinantia lacks that Commelina spathe pocket and carries its flowers on an open terminal cyme.

images.role: Side view — exposed cyme above an open leaflike bract
images.caption: Trace the stalk from the open flower past the buds to the broad green bract below the cluster. The bract spreads outward instead of enclosing the entire cluster in a fused Commelina-style pocket. The boatlike green coverings immediately around individual buds are sepals; do not confuse those with a spathe.
